planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun for the brightest foliage color; check state and local regulations before planting, as Japanese barberry is classified as invasive or restricted in a number of states.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun, where the foliage color develops most intensely; in hot-summer climates or with too much shade the leaves fade toward chartreuse-green and can scorch in reflected heat, so avoid siting against south-facing walls in the deep South. Golden Barberry is a rounded, thorny, deciduous shrub prized for foliage that emerges bright yellow in spring and holds a warm chartreuse-gold through summer, contrasting sharply with dark-leaved companions and lighting up shaded corners of a border. Small pale-yellow flowers appear along the stems in mid-spring, followed by bright red berries that persist into winter and provide food for birds. Established plants need only an occasional shaping prune and tolerate heat, drought, and poor soil, but because Japanese barberry cultivars readily naturalize in woodland edges across much of the eastern and midwestern US, gardeners should confirm local planting restrictions first.

common_name: Helmond Pillar Barberry (Narrow Columnar Purple-Red Barberry)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; the strictly upright, columnar habit makes it useful for narrow side yards and vertical accents where a spreading barberry would not fit, and it holds its shape with little to no pruning.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun; the deep reddish-purple color is most intense with maximum light exposure. Helmond Pillar is a distinctive narrow, upright barberry that grows as a tight column rather than a mound, making it valuable as a vertical accent, a living exclamation point in a mixed border, or a tidy screen along a narrow side yard where wide-spreading barberries won't fit. Small pale-yellow flowers open along the thorny reddish-brown stems in spring, followed by elongated red berries in fall that persist into winter. It needs almost no shaping to maintain its columnar form and, once established, tolerates heat, drought, and poor soil, though gardeners should confirm Japanese barberry is not restricted in their state before planting.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; wintergreen barberry keeps its glossy, spine-edged foliage year-round, unlike the more commonly planted deciduous Japanese barberry cultivars.

directions: Plant in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; flowering and fruiting are heaviest in more sun, but the evergreen foliage stays dense and glossy even in partial shade. Wintergreen Barberry is an evergreen Chinese species with stiff, spiny, dark green leaves up to three inches long that can take on a bronze or wine tint in cold winters, arranged along thorny stems armed with sharp three-parted spines. Clusters of small, fragrant, lemon-yellow flowers open in late spring, followed by blue-black berries that persist into winter and draw songbirds. Its dense, thorny branching makes it one of the best barrier or security hedge plants available, forming an almost impenetrable screen with minimal pruning once established.

common_name: Northern Gold Forsythia (Extreme Cold-Hardy Ottawa Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Northern Gold was bred at the Ottawa Research Station from a Forsythia ovata cross specifically for flower-bud hardiness in prairie and northern winters.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the heaviest bloom. Northern Gold was developed in Ottawa from a Forsythia ovata cross specifically to survive winter cold that kills the flower buds of common border forsythia, so it reliably covers itself in golden-yellow flowers in early spring even after severe northern winters. The vigorous, upright, arching shrub grows into a large informal specimen or hedge and adapts to a wide range of soils once established. Prune immediately after flowering to shape or control size, since old wood carries next year's flower buds and later pruning sacrifices bloom.

common_name: Beatrix Farrand Forsythia (Large-Flowered Arnold Arboretum Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; give Beatrix Farrand ample room, since it grows into one of the largest and most vigorous of the border forsythia cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for maximum flowering. Beatrix Farrand, introduced from the Arnold Arboretum in the 1940s and named for the noted landscape architect, is valued for individual flowers noticeably larger and deeper golden-yellow than most other border forsythia cultivars, opening in dense clusters along the bare stems in early spring before the leaves emerge. It grows quickly into a large, vigorous, arching shrub well suited to big borders, screens, or informal hedges where its size is an asset rather than a liability. Prune right after flowering to control size and shape, since flower buds form on the current season's wood and later pruning removes next spring's display.

common_name: Vermont Sun Forsythia (Extreme Bud-Hardy Manchurian Forsythia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter or early spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; Vermont Sun was selected at the University of Vermont for flower buds that survive temperatures down to roughly -25 deg F, among the hardiest of any forsythia.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun. Vermont Sun is a selection of the Manchurian forsythia bred at the University of Vermont for outstanding flower-bud hardiness, opening its bright yellow flowers earlier in the season than most border forsythia and reliably blooming even after winters that damage the buds of less hardy types. It has an upright habit and larger, broader leaves than common forsythia, giving it a coarser but still attractive summer presence after the spring flower display fades. It is an excellent choice for the coldest northern gardens where more familiar Forsythia x intermedia cultivars bloom sparsely or fail to flower at all; prune immediately after flowering since buds form on old wood.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in loamy, moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun and a sheltered site; unlike the familiar Buddleja davidii, this species blooms on old wood, so prune only lightly right after flowering.

directions: Plant in loamy, moist, fertile, well-drained soil in a sheltered, full-sun site; this South American species dislikes both drought stress and waterlogged soil, so consistent moisture during establishment matters more than for the drought-tough Buddleja davidii. Orange Ball Tree is instantly recognizable for its tight, perfectly round clusters of yellowish-orange flowers held at the branch tips in early summer, a striking departure from the elongated flower spikes of most other butterfly bushes, and the semi-evergreen, dark green, narrow leaves add structure into winter in milder climates. Because it flowers on wood formed the previous year, prune only right after the bloom period to shape the shrub without sacrificing next year's display. Its fragrant, unusually shaped flowers are heavily visited by bees and butterflies and make it a good specimen or background shrub for a sheltered border.

common_name: Harlequin Butterfly Bush (Variegated Cream-Edged Magenta Buddleja)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun; deadhead spent flower spikes through the season to prolong bloom, and cut the whole shrub back hard in late winter since it flowers on new wood.

directions: Plant in average, well-drained soil in full sun, where the cream-margined foliage colors best and flowering is heaviest. Harlequin is a variegated-leaf butterfly bush cultivar with gray-green leaves irregularly edged in creamy white, giving the plant garden interest even between bloom cycles, topped from midsummer into fall with fragrant, rich magenta-purple flower spikes that draw butterflies and hummingbirds in large numbers. It stays more compact than the species type, making it a good choice for smaller borders where its two-tone foliage can be appreciated up close. Cut the shrub back hard to 12-18 inches in late winter each year to keep it dense and floriferous, since flowers form only on the current season's growth.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun; this hybrid blooms on new wood, so an annual hard cutback to a foot or so above the ground in late winter keeps it compact and encourages the heaviest flowering.

directions: Plant in well-drained, average to fertile soil in full sun, and cut the shrub back hard each late winter since flowers form on new growth. Honeycomb is a Buddleja x weyeriana cultivar prized for its rounded clusters of warm golden-yellow flowers touched with orange at the eye, a distinctive color break from the purples, pinks, and whites typical of most butterfly bushes, opening from midsummer through the first hard frost. The gracefully arching branches and gray-green, lance-shaped leaves give it a looser, more informal habit than compact davidii cultivars, and its long, fragrant bloom season makes it a strong magnet for butterflies, bees, and hummingbirds. In colder parts of its range it may die back to the ground in winter but regrows vigorously and flowers well the same season.

planting.note: Plant rooted cuttings or container shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Chinese abelia is the wild species behind the widely planted Abelia x grandiflora hybrid and blooms with a stronger fragrance than that hybrid.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; flowering is heaviest in more sun, but the arching habit and fragrance hold up well in a partly shaded border. Chinese Abelia is the wild parent species behind the far more common Abelia x grandiflora hybrid, distinguished by an especially long early-summer-to-fall bloom of small, tubular, intensely fragrant white flowers set off by showy pink calyces that persist after the petals drop, extending the display well beyond the actual flowering period. Its arching, multi-stemmed habit and fine-textured deciduous foliage give it a graceful, informal form well suited to a mixed shrub border or naturalized planting. Established plants are moderately drought tolerant and need only an occasional shaping prune after flowering to maintain a tidy form.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (Royal Horticultural Society)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade; Funshine is a slow-growing, compact sport valued for foliage color rather than flower size.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun to partial shade. Funshine is a compact, slow-growing glossy abelia selection grown chiefly for its foliage, which emerges a glowing apricot-orange in spring before settling into tones of gold, chartreuse, and green through the growing season, giving the low mounded shrub color impact even without its lavender-pink summer flowers. Its dense, fill-to-the-ground habit works well as a low border or foundation planting without needing facer plants in front, and it holds its bright coloring in both sun and part shade. Established plants need only light shaping after the main flowering flush and are drought tolerant, low-maintenance shrubs once rooted in.

common_name: Sweet Emotion Abelia (Extreme Cold-Hardy Fragrant Abelia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or spring in average, moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Sweet Emotion was selected for flower-bud hardiness to USDA zone 4, extending fragrant abelia into much colder gardens than the species is normally grown.

directions: Plant in average, moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; this selection does not perform as well in hot, humid summer climates as it does in cooler northern gardens. Sweet Emotion is a cold-hardy selection of fragrant abelia bred for reliable performance into USDA zone 4, well beyond the range of most abelias, forming a dense, rounded, deciduous shrub covered in mid to late spring with clusters of two-toned tubular flowers that open from deep pink buds to white or pale pink. Its jasmine-like fragrance is considered the strongest of any abelia, carrying well beyond the shrub itself, and glossy green summer foliage turns orange-red in fall before dropping. Prune lightly right after flowering to maintain shape, since next year's blooms form on the current season's growth.
